entries.title: ‘Who would dare take on Elizabeth Jane Howard’s fans?’ Louisa Young on reviving the Cazalet Chronicles
entries.summary: The author’s new trilogy continues her aunt’s beloved family saga. What would happen next to the sprawling cast of characters ... and could she pull it off? In the late 1980s Elizabeth Jane Howard was wondering what to write next. Jane, as she was always known, was at that time the author of seven novels. Her debut, The Beautiful Visit, had won the John Llewellyn Rhys prize in 1951 when she was 28
entries.content:
In the late 1980s Elizabeth Jane Howard was wondering what to write next. Jane, as she was always known, was at that time the author of seven novels. Her debut, The Beautiful Visit, had won the John Llewellyn Rhys prize in 1951 when she was 28 years old and The Long View (1956) was one of the first novels written with reverse chronology. Her talent was somewhat overshadowed in a tawdry world by her drop-dead beauty and by her having briefly been an actor (and by the famous lovers and husbands she walked out on, including Sir Peter Scott, the ornithologist and conservationist, in 1946, and Kingsley Amis, who was then himself a famous novelist, in 1983).

Stuck, she asked her stepson Martin Amis which of two projects she should go for: an updated version of Sense and Sensibility, or a family saga based on her own life? He said, do the family saga. Jane’s family project developed into the Cazalet Chronicles: five volumes in which she fictionalised her life’s experience, divided between three young female cousins, Polly, Clary and Louise, and a cast of 52 more named characters, set between London and a grandparental family home in Sussex.

The first volume, The Light Years (1990), opens in 1937, and the series closes in 1958. From a slow beginning, the Cazalets grew into a worldwide phenomenon, selling millions of copies, and has been in print ever since.

As each one came out I tore through them: not just because Jane was brilliant and I was a fan, but also because she was my aunt. My grandmother, the sculptor Kathleen Scott, had been Jane’s mother-in-law: mother of Peter Scott and of my father Wayland Young. In 1990 I was writing a biography of Kathleen – so Jane was a living witness for me. It put my smoky-voiced, glamorous aunt and me in a peculiar overlap: she, in her 60s, was writing a fictional version of the actual life she had lived, and I, at 29, was writing a putatively factual version of the same things, though they had happened before I was born.

That was my first book; the last Cazalet novel was to be Jane’s last. I was so ready to sit at her feet, listen to her stories, to “carry her reticule”, as she put it, when she went to literary festivals. In her beautiful house in Bungay, Suffolk, where she lived with her brother Colin, known as Monkey, we talked about everything. How funny life is, how circular! We gossiped about people I’d never met, from decades before my birth. Jane gave me one version; Monkey gave me another. She loved me, I think, at least initially, for my dad’s sake, and because I was a young woman, becoming a writer.

Through the mirrors and veils of her fiction, I recognised people and situations, saw hints of truth about my own family’s mysteries. In reality, Kathleen Scott and 19-year-old Jane had not got on at all – it was a hurried and frightened wartime marriage, a failure immediately. In the Cazalet books, Kathleen is fictionalised as Zee and comes across as an absolute monster, who threatened to kill Jane/Louise.

But my father adored his mother: “She was always saying she was going to kill people!” he said. “It was a turn of phrase … but the wrong one for Jane then.” My own mother had been secretary to Peter (fictionalised as Michael Hadleigh), and had lent the penniless Jane money to leave him. Both the real people and the characters in the books, only in their twenties, overlapped during and after the war in west London, where I lived. The past seemed so close, and so far away. And of course it’s always fascinating to think of your parents’ generation being young, and messy.

I read the volumes avidly as they came out, and ran back to her wanting to ask, “Jane, is that real? Was that true?” But these can be hard questions, and impertinent. Fiction is meant to be emotionally true, not factually. “True in spirit,” she told me. At the same time as she protected her own version, she wanted to protect those she loved. This curious palimpsest gives the fiction an astonishing extra tension, as those who have read her memoir, Slipstream (2002), or the biography by Artemis Cooper (A Dangerous Innocence, 2016) can testify.

The Cazalet Chronicles are often described as a comfort read, both because they contain servants and food and clothes, and because they provide such a deeply complete fictional world for escaping into from an unsatisfactory real one. But being upper-middle-class doesn’t protect the characters from rape, child abuse, incest, abandonment, suicide, divorce, concentration camps, war, fear, loss, cancer or death. They are sometimes seen as somehow lighter than her earlier, more literary works, but she didn’t think they were, and they’re not: I’ve read them many times now and each time they get darker. Their surge of popularity during Covid makes perfect sense to me: the characters, like the rest of us during the lockdowns, were restricted by events beyond their control. They couldn’t go where they wanted; they couldn’t be with who they wanted to be with, they were constrained and scared and bored. And, in the main, they survived. Which is always reassuring.

When something works, we want more of it. I always wanted more Cazalets. Chronicles should go on. But it never crossed my mind to imagine I could pick up Jane’s mantle. Until it did – which was as a PS in a “What Next?” email of my own to my agent. I was suggesting a long list of bad ideas, and then at the end: “Or I could always try to continue the Cazalet Chronicles”. It was a joke! Jane was a great writer. Who would dare face the ranks of devotees, still so dedicated and protective? Or launch into the continuity perils of 500,000 words?

I realised it wasn’t such a terrible idea when Jane’s daughter, my cousin, gave her blessing. I found a message from Jane telling me a novel of mine was “a triumph”. My agent was all for it. We went to Jane’s own publishers, and worked with some of her editors. There would be three volumes, we decided. One would just be silly – why wake everybody up for that? – and more than three was too far ahead to see.

I read the books again, thinking about how I would do it. Loose ends trailed before me, begging to be picked up. Pitfalls beckoned. The unsettling incestuous romance between half-siblings Juliet and Neville needed closure. Villy, Louise’s mother, was a victim of being a 20th-century woman as well as being a bad mother. Mainly because she had to have all her teeth out, I wanted her to have a better ending than just being dumped and her four children disliking her. Virtuous, kind Rachel, who for years didn’t even realise she was a lesbian, deserved better too (I am regularly accosted by young gay women wanting to know what I have planned for her, because it had better be good). And then there is the great unresolved issue of Louise’s abandoned son, Sebastian, who was too close to home in reality for Jane to address in fiction. And look, there’s my fictionalised grandparents, Zee and The Judge; there’s fictionalised Dad, here called Hugo, disguised as a cousin for propriety’s sake. It was these novels that told me how much Jane had loved Dad. Alas, she had him die in the War, and this is not the kind of saga where he can come back to life played by a different actor. (In reality he had six children and a sixty-year marriage, and lived till 2009.)

It did seem to me that the characters were all still there, their lives continuing, just off-stage. The fifth Cazalet book, All Change, ends at Christmas 1958. I was born three months later. I was there! The idea that their lives might be up to me and my imagination was intoxicating, trepidation-inducing and inspiring. It’s not about inventing things to happen to them: they are already in full flow. I am chasing after them with a notebook. I make it seamless for the reader by continuing Jane’s elegant structure of tessellated sections, each from one person’s point of view, but I do allow the way I write, my generation’s use of language, to bring things forward in time, as time itself moves forward.

I’m now the age Jane was when she was writing this fictionalised account of her life. Can these three novels count as mine, when I’ve broken into her world to write them? I’m not sure that’s answerable. But equally, what a circle it is, from writing about the young girl Jane in my biography of my grandmother, to the picking up of her baton now, after her death, beyond her knowledge. By bringing these characters on, of necessity I make them mine. Because this isn’t a pastiche, an imitation, or a homage. It’s a living story. The family chronicle rolls on through time in reality as it does on the page. I might even put it in a book …

entries.title: Could this policy fix the care system and slash student debt at the same time?
entries.summary: Andy Burnham is in need of radical proposals. A ‘care first’ year in exchange for 50% off fees could be just what he needsThe UK’s social care sector is in crisis. Costs are spiralling, with many local councils forced to dedicate the vast majority of their budgets to it. At the same time, more and more families are seeing their savings disappear into the black hole of nursing home fees. With an ag
entries.content:
The UK’s social care sector is in crisis. Costs are spiralling, with many local councils forced to dedicate the vast majority of their budgets to it. At the same time, more and more families are seeing their savings disappear into the black hole of nursing home fees. With an ageing population, the problem is set to get worse.

In only his second week as prime minister, Andy Burnham pledged to succeed where so many of his predecessors have failed: by fixing Britain’s social care system. And yet, as parliament returns from recess, the new-ish administration is still worryingly unclear about how it will do this. Despite Burnham declaring that care workers should enjoy better compensation, we don’t know how he plans to pay for any of it – not least because he has kept Starmer’s campaign pledge to not raise income tax, VAT or national insurance. At the moment, it looks as though it will be impossible to square the circle.

What the government needs is big, innovative ideas. We should look to history for inspiration, while also absorbing the lessons of past mistakes.

How about national service – but instead of entering the military, recruits are pledged to the NHS? Eye-catching, but ultimately not right, at least not in that form. Forcing young people to do work they’d prefer not to, when there isn’t even an enemy at the gates, will only lead to bad results. Indeed, the army has already learned this: compulsory recruits in the postwar period were typically unmotivated and incompetent; a drag rather than a boost to the military’s performance.

But that’s a crude precedent. We can take more relevant inspiration from elsewhere. For example, young men in Austria who do not wish to serve in the military can instead opt for health or social care work; many end up driving ambulances. The trade-off is that they do nine months instead of six. In Norway, conscientious objectors were, until 2012, able to perform “civilian national service”, working in community settings such as primary schools or nursing homes, and accruing points towards university entry for doing so.

Thinking along similar lines, how about this? The government offers recent school leavers a deal: 50% off their total university fees if they first spend a year volunteering in social care. (You could even up the ante: 100% off if they commit to two years; full back pay with a bonus if they stay in the profession.)

There are many reasons to take this proposal seriously. First, it is not just social care that is in crisis. University funding is, too. Right now, UK universities are panicking because student enrolment fees no longer keep them in the black. But at the same time, undergraduates are being presented with eye-watering loan bills and interest rates at levels that make capital repayment much harder. We are rapidly approaching a cliff edge. The government is going to have to fix the system one way or the other. Why not do something innovative and radical at the same time?

The overall maths might work surprisingly well. If uptake is sufficiently high, the state gets an enormous amount of free (in the short term) labour to offset the costs of lost loan revenue. If that sounds exploitative, remember that it would be in the interests of young people themselves (in the longer term) because they would leave university with a heck of a lot less debt.

But the upsides go beyond just money. At the moment, unscrupulous agencies too often rely on low-paid migrant labour, ignoring the linguistic and caring skills required do a safe and competent job. A scheme like this would open up a new pool for recruitment – of eager-to-learn young people at the start of their careers.

Of course, they would have to undergo proper training and would only get the discount if they complete the programme to a certified high level. Along the way, some would discover that care work can be deeply rewarding; that the current stigmatisation of this kind of employment just doesn’t tally with reality.

I know, because since I broke my neck in a rock-climbing accident in 2023, I have relied on 24-hour live-in care. I am lucky to be with a very good agency, which only employs highly competent and conscientious staff (from all over the world). I have seen up close just how rewarding and dignified care work can be. Sure, there are some icky parts to looking after a man who can’t go to the toilet by himself. But all my care workers take real pride in helping me live as close to a normal life as possible. Of course, they’re not on footballers’ wages. But they get a very visible amount of life satisfaction from helping me find mine.

One of the most interesting care workers I’ve met was covering holiday earlier in the summer. Originally from Ireland, she had just finished a two-year master’s degree at King’s College London (by coincidence where I teach, in a different department). She is now a qualified dietitian, who in future will be working in hospitals. But until she makes that transition she is spending a year with my spinal agency, after having been employed as a care worker in Ireland for two years prior to her degree. It’s a job she finds deeply rewarding.

I am confident that if we incentivised UK students to try social care before university, many would consider rejoining once they had graduated. This would help to reduce wider stigma around care work as the preserve of poor, often vulnerable migrant workers, assumed to be doing it only because no one else will.

Look, I’m neither a government accountant nor a policy expert. Perhaps when we’ve crunched the numbers, it just doesn’t work. But from where I’m sitting this has the potential to be a win-win of the sort that could define the Burnham administration. All the scheme needs is a name, and there’s an obvious one for the taking: “Care First”.

Dr Paul Sagar is a reader in political theory at King’s College London.

Further reading

Labours of Love: The Crisis of Care by Madeleine Bunting (Granta, £9.99)

The Courage to Care: Nurses, Families and Hope by Christie Watson (Vintage, £10.99)

Who Cares by Emily Kenway (Headline, £12.99)

entries.title: How to make a bestseller: insiders reveal the tricks of the book trade
entries.summary: From cover design to shelf placement and influencer partnerships … how publishers will persuade you to buy their books this autumnThink about the last book you bought. How did you choose it? Was it from a recommendation, a review, a TikTok video? Did the cover grab you, were you swayed by the quotes on the front, or did you just happen to spot it on an appealing table as you walked into the shop?
entries.content:
Think about the last book you bought. How did you choose it? Was it from a recommendation, a review, a TikTok video? Did the cover grab you, were you swayed by the quotes on the front, or did you just happen to spot it on an appealing table as you walked into the shop? Did you think about all the nudges that led you to that decision – by the publisher, the bookseller or that person you follow on Insta?

The reality is that our reading choices are directed and massaged at every turn. “It’s all about the art of persuasion,” says Philip Gwyn Jones, who was a publisher for more than 30 years and is now a literary agent. And who are the persuaders? They’re the booksellers, the supermarket stock buyers, the publishing houses and their ranks of marketers and publicists. And, more recently, persuasion often comes from BookTokers and online influencers, social media videos, podcasts and Instagram posts. How is all this changing publishing?

We all judge books to some extent by their covers, but did you know how much thought goes into finding just the right cover, colour, font and design? These covers are focus-grouped, shown to supermarket buyers and often changed at their behest, according to Jamie Keenan, one of Britain’s leading book designers. “That happens quite a lot,” he says. “If Tesco with commercial books, or Waterstones with literary stuff, don’t like it, they’ve got a tremendous amount of clout.” (Waterstones and Tesco declined to speak to me for this piece.)

Meanwhile, online browsing and buying have brought about big changes. “There’s been a move towards more iconic book covers because of thumbnail images [on apps and websites],” Keenan explains. “One very simple emblem or logo that you can see from a distance, even when it’s two inches tall. Nice bright colours and big type,” he adds. “That’s what publishers are doing to attract people’s attention.”

It’s true: when I went into Waterstones last week, I felt like reaching for my sunglasses to shield the glare of garish, saturated colours screaming from the fiction shelves: more sweet shop than book store. When I shared a photo on Instagram, a number of authors messaged me. “I hate it,” said one (whose own latest novel has a brightly coloured cover). “It’s just so brash.” Yet ironically, because all these books look the same, the effect is to make them blend in, not stand out. “Jewel tones have the industry in a headlock,” messaged another.

And then there are the increasing numbers of copycat covers, so that every cosy crime novel suddenly looks like Richard Osman’s bestsellers – cream background, coloured border, hand-lettering – and all heartwarming Japanese books have to feature a cat. (At his last publishing house, says Gwyn Jones, for Japanese fiction “there was this unspoken imperative to put a cat on the cover even if there wasn’t a major role for a cat in the book. It did seem to make a difference.”) “You quite often get briefs on what are called comparable titles,” Keenan says. “That’s a nod-and-a-wink way of saying, ‘Can you do something that looks a bit like these three?’”

After the cover does its trick, we read the publisher’s description on the back. That’s the work of copywriters. “The cover designer has got them to pick up the book,” says a copywriter for a major commercial publisher. “It’s my job to make sure they don’t put it down again.”

The blurb is how we decide if this book is one for us. “You’ve got seconds to grab people,” says the copywriter. One of their tricks is to use Christopher Booker’s book The Seven Basic Plots. “Most stories can fit into three or four of Booker’s categories: The Quest, Overcoming the Monster and so on. It gives you tools to tell the story of the book in different ways. You want to say: ‘It’s the same but different.’”

What if an author isn’t writing what’s on trend right now? “For the best part of two decades,” the copywriter says, “we had Scandi noir: very dark, psychological thrillers. Now cosy crime is absolutely everything. If a writer is still writing noir and wants their books to be in the supermarkets, it needs to look like the books that are selling in supermarkets.” That means “you’ll find books being packaged rather differently to how they [really] are”. These cosy crime blurbs need to, frankly, make death and violence sound like a minor inconvenience, so they focus on the mystery aspect (the books are “ingenious”, full of “twists and turns”) or the welcoming narrative tone (“delicious’” and “delightful”) or the sense of tradition they follow as “quintessentially British” stories. But “publishers are lemmings,” the copywriter says, “and that’s where the market is.”

“There has been a sense since the mid-2000s that popular fiction readers’ tastes have narrowed,” they continue, “following one or two big trends. That parallels [the rise of] social media. Romantasy and cosy crime are the main areas of current growth.”

Whatever the genre, “a blurb has to tell a little story,” says Louise Willder, another copywriter, and author of a book on the subject, Blurb Your Enthusiasm. But, “we’re aware not every word we write will get read.” That’s because, explains the commercial copywriter, “People read in an ‘F’ [shape] – they’ll read across the top and then they won’t read the next line, they’ll just drop down to the next paragraph. So you’re trying to hit your marks at the start of each paragraph.” Cliches have always been rampant, they just shift with time. So “witty” becomes “whip-smart”. “It’s never ‘moving’, it has to be ‘deeply moving’,” says Willder.

Publishers’ blurbs aren’t the only thing on book covers; they are also clogged with endorsements from fellow authors. According to Willder, “audiences say they’re mistrustful” of these. There’s a sense that they are favours for friends – which may be justified. When it comes to quotes, “networking is crucial” confirms the commercial copywriter. “I’ll try to get two or three endorsements from my circles, or the author’s circles,” adds Gwyn Jones.

Author endorsements are, in any event, more often aimed at booksellers than readers. Even though many books are now sold online, the visibility of books in shops remains crucial to their success. Although some names may offer more effective badging than others – certain authors “seem to pop up on every single book”, says Brett Wolstencroft, manager at independent chain Daunt Books. “Stephen King has endorsed so many people,” says the commercial copywriter. “Tony Parsons is another culprit.”

Not all booksellers need to be persuaded, it should be said – some need to be paid. One experienced publicist I spoke to said: “To get books into supermarkets, you have to pay quite a lot of money. The general public thinks that those top 10s are earned positions and they are very much not earned positions. They’re paid for.” This practice used to be widespread. TG Jones, formerly WH Smith, also charged publishers for chart space, according to a 2022 BBC report, though the chain said that sales performance was also a factor. And in the time before James Daunt took over, Waterstones charged publishers to put their books on display tables. But now, one Waterstones bookseller tells me, “everything is down to individual booksellers”.

Publishers send out early copies of books to booksellers, because if they read and like them, they can kickstart a book’s success. Books need advocates, and booksellers are among the finest. Wolstencroft tells me that “the public trust us [as booksellers] because they know we really have read these books, we really do like them, we’re not driven by the tricks of the publisher.”

But what about the tricks of the bookseller? Three of the four window displays in Daunt’s Marylebone branch are each focused on one title. “People have a very limited attention span,” Wolstencroft says. “Give them a wall of different books and they’ll move on quite quickly.”

Conversations with customers – hand-selling books – are crucial, because “they’re not just talking to one person, but to 30, 40 people around them in the shop. And the business of hearing a book recommended is incredibly powerful,” Wolstencroft adds. “Three or four people will come to the till in the next five minutes with that book.”

In many bookshops, a surrogate for hand-selling books are the cards attached to shelves praising particular books – shelf talkers, as they’re known. The Waterstones bookseller tells me that these “go a long way if they read sincerely. If they’re short and just say ‘I love this book’ or ‘It really made me cry’, that will work almost 100% of the time. One that doesn’t feel emotional will never work.” Waterstones, however, has a “standard that there have to be three review cards per bay [of shelves], so sometimes you have to churn them out to fill the bay. And if nobody [in the shop] has read it, you just steal something off Goodreads.” Those cards, they admit, “are less successful”.

“Enthusiasm is the thing that sells,” the bookseller tells me. “People often ask for recommendations and you’re supposed to go for the [Waterstones] book of the month, [but] I like to recommend things I actually want people to read.” Smaller independent bookshops can manage personal recommendations via tailored book subscription services. “I don’t really use the word subscription,” says David Headley, who runs Goldsboro Books in London and Brighton. “We call it a book club, with members rather than subscribers.”

Goldsboro has four book clubs, each sending out a new work of fiction in an exclusive edition to its members every month, including clubs for fantasy (with 2,000 members) and a recently launched club for debut fiction, with almost 500 members. Numbers like these give Goldsboro’s clubs tremendous clout. Being chosen for one of them – Headley picks the books himself – “can get you into the top 10 bestsellers”, he tells me.

How does he choose the books? “I go into publishers every six months and they pitch their books that are coming out.” But the final choice is Headley’s, and publishers don’t contribute to the cost. “We pay for everything, so if I buy 2,000 books, I have to sell them.”

Headley is also a literary agent, and several of his own client authors have appeared as Goldsboro book club choices. How does that work? “Not every author gets that privilege,” he says. “I don’t ever take on a client and promise them that. But if I really love the book and think people should read it, then I’ll choose it.”

What publishers are always chasing is the elusive word-of-mouth recommendation, an artificial version of a trusted friend pressing a favourite new book on you. That’s what can be provided by booksellers and, increasingly, online influencers, on platforms such as TikTok and YouTube. “Influencers are important because they talk to a community and they’re trusted by the community,” says Lee Dibble, digital marketing director at Pan Macmillan. “Jack Edwards [who has 1.6 million followers on YouTube and 1.2 million on Instagram] or Dua Lipa can create huge interest from nowhere,” adds Gwyn Jones. See, for example, how Edwards put a rocket under Fyodor Dostoevsky in 2024, helping the obscure novella White Nights shift more than 100,000 copies.

How do publishers persuade influencers to cover their books? “You might gather influencers round a restaurant table,” says Gwyn Jones. For books that publishers have spent a lot of money on, the process begins early. “Big dinners a year and a half ahead of publication,” a publicist tells me. “If it’s a debut they’ll invite [the debut author] alongside lots of established names to draw the [influencers] in.”

“You’re trying to buy their favour,” says Gwyn Jones of the influencers. In some cases, the buying is literal: “There are some BookTokers who expect to get paid to review books,” says the publicist. “It feels like you’re breaking some sort of contract there.” It is not, they add, about securing a positive review. “It’s more that it’s so competitive, some people think they can charge just to cover your book.”

This is separate from paid partnerships, where, as Dibble puts it, “they have to make it really clear they’ve been paid for that work” and “there might be a brief where there’s a couple of messages [the publisher] wants to get across, but it’s completely up to them how they talk about it”.

It’s arguable, however, that any paid advert by an influencer muddies the waters of that crucial trust relationship with their community. “The whole thing of it being a common endeavour sort of dies the minute you start charging for your services,” says Gwyn Jones. Search Instagram or TikTok for “books” and “ad” and you’ll find numerous book influencers with text such as: “my fave author has a new book out and it is one of her best” or “this series felt like three arrows in the chest”. If they’re being paid to post this, how can their followers be sure it’s a sincerely held opinion?

Publicists are the publisher’s frontline in seeking to secure attention for their books, but even this has changed in the digital age. “There’s an old adage where you have to see [the book] seven times before you buy it, so you’re trying to cover as many bases as you can,” the publicist tells me. As well as space in traditional media, this means social media (“a huge part” of publicity now) and new media. “If you can get an author on a really big podcast, that book can go to number one,” the publicist says. And “the big podcasts for books aren’t podcasts about books – The News Agents, Fearne Cotton’s Happy Place, or Davina McCall. You’re trying to pull out the lifestyle angles.”

Some traditions persist: “I stand by the fact,” the publicist tells me, “that there is no such thing as bad publicity. When there was all the controversy over The Salt Path, sales actually went up.”

There are areas that remain largely out of publishers’ control, such as Amazon. But they do have some techniques. Publishers now usually add subtitles to a book on Amazon (“For readers of Sally Rooney”) to try to draw stray web searches. They also tag books with keywords. But it only goes so far. “You won’t show up next to Richard Osman by mentioning him 100 times in the metadata,” Dibble says.

If you’ve ever wondered why your favourite author is constantly urging you on social media to pre-order their new book, it’s because “the impact of Amazon rankings is huge”, the publicist tells me. “Preordering can have the biggest impact, and then it’s much easier to stay [in the charts] because it’s a snowball effect.” And where once search engine optimisation (SEO) was the big thing, now it’s GEO – generative engine optimisation, or “making sure our books are discoverable by chat bots”, Dibble says. So how do you court ChatGPT or Claude? It’s an evolving science, she says, but “you can format your content in particular ways that bots like, such as author Q&As or listicles”.

Are prizes still important? “Definitely, absolutely,” says Philip Gwyn Jones. “You’ve got to make choices and prizes help people make choices.” It is, of course, not possible to sway prize juries, but there are other tools available. “You think about the kind of people who get put on prize juries and review regularly and you send the book to them,” says Gwyn Jones. You decide, as a publisher, which books to submit: “an exercise in diplomacy, as you can imagine … A publisher’s responsibility is to manage it in such a way that it doesn’t cause any outlandish hissy fits.”

“Those meetings can get really heated,” agrees the publicist, who adds that another tool in their armoury is to “strategically publish books so they tie in with eligibility periods for book prizes”.

But what came across time and again from the people I spoke to is how authenticity is key. “It’s not like Quaker Oats,” says one publicist. “You’ve got to be passionate.” “I would only pitch things that are genuinely good,” says another. “Trust is the important thing,” David Headley adds.

All of these techniques can help to give a book a leg up, but nothing guarantees success even then. “We’re always quoting [screenwriter] William Goldman,” says Louise Willder. “‘Nobody knows anything.’” In the end, as readers and browsers, despite all the nudges and cajolery and the tricks of the trade, the final decision really is ours.

entries.title: Sophie, Standing There by Meg Mason review – a tale of literary obsession, with cameos from real-life authors
entries.summary: A heartbroken woman becomes fixated on a famous writer in this witty, touching follow-up to Sorrow and BlissThe protagonist of Meg Mason’s new book, the follow-up to the 2020 tragicomedy Sorrow and Bliss, is an invisible woman. She might well be standing there but you won’t notice her. She’s a techie at literary festivals – the person who shuffles up to a famous writer a few minutes before their e
entries.content:
The protagonist of Meg Mason’s new book, the follow-up to the 2020 tragicomedy Sorrow and Bliss, is an invisible woman. She might well be standing there but you won’t notice her. She’s a techie at literary festivals – the person who shuffles up to a famous writer a few minutes before their event and apologetically slides a microphone cable down their shirt while they’re making small talk with the chair or accepting a bottle of room-temperature mineral water from an anxious publicist.

No man is a hero to his valet, and no writer is a hero to the technical staff lurking in the wings of a venue. Mason’s opening pages present a teasing but not quite libellous series of cameos from real writers: George Saunders deciding at an inconsiderately late stage to insist on swapping his headset for a lapel mic; Ann Patchett being frosty with a fan; Mick Herron accidentally stepping on someone’s foot and not apologising.

Sophie lurks in the wings of her own life, too. She likes her job but she has much to be sad about. Not long ago, her husband brought their relationship to an end with oafish callousness (she was in the shower; he didn’t bother to take his earbuds out while he delivered the news), and with it her hope of becoming a mother. Now her beloved books are in storage in the garage of her old house and she’s living alone in a dingy rental flat owned by her husband: “The water in Sophie’s glass tasted like pipes. She felt very tired … The coffee table was actually a cable spool with ‘12 AWG’ spray-painted on the drum.”

Mason’s prose is wan and witty, handling the admixture of pathos and bathos well; and her sinuous sentences capture the wavering movements of thought with less fuss and more laughs than, say, Virginia Woolf. As a bookish person, and one inhabiting a lightly metafictional narrative, Sophie is glumly aware of her literary analogues. There’s “a lot of sad girl fiction” on her Kindle. “Eleanor Oliphant,” she reflects. “That was the worst. Even though it was extremely well written and Sophie had recommended it to about 10 people when it first came out, in this moment, she wished she’d never heard of it and couldn’t recall the cheese scones and those cappuccinos Eleanor always ordered, the saddest of all the coffees.”

Mason is brilliant, too, at describing the small but intense joys of everyday life – getting your scalp massaged at the hairdresser, for instance, or owning one really nicely designed pair of trousers. She’s likewise good at life’s routine humiliations and inanities, such as bumping into your ex with a leaky bottle of coconut water in your handbag, or asking a favour from someone whose text messages you have been ignoring, or realising how much it’s going to cost to take an Uber back from Ikea.

The engine of the plot is a parasocial relationship but an old-fashioned one: Sophie becomes obsessed with a famous writer. (The writer is just “the author” for the first part of the book but then, perhaps finding the conceit unwieldy, Mason gives her a name, Lilac Dunne.) Sophie rereads her books, talks to an imaginary version of Lilac, and spends hours scrolling images of her and listening to her on podcasts. Then fantasy and reality collide when, to Sophie’s terror, Lilac is booked to appear after Elizabeth Strout drops out of an event.

An infatuation with the idea of Lilac, with her public persona and her authorial voice, is complicated by a first glancing and then apparently deepening encounter with the real thing. Lilac takes Sophie up, a little, and Sophie is flattered and flustered. She thinks of herself as a nobody but Lilac seems not to. And then … well, no spoilers.

If there’s a fault to be identified in this continuously witty and touching narrative, it’s in the person of Lilac. As a writer she appears to be unstuffy, poised, wise and at ease in the world; Sophie isn’t the only one to fall for her. When we encounter Lilac in person, she’s harder and more ruthless than her public persona but no less impenetrable, with none of the psychological complexity or vulnerability displayed elsewhere. She’s more deus ex machina in Sophie’s story than fully realised character.

But perhaps that’s by design. In this Bridget-Jones-meets-Pirandello caper, Mason is nothing if not knowing. As she writes in one of the closing chapters, opening a little postmodern mise en abyme: “If someone wrote a novel about Sophie, which they wouldn’t, but if they did, it could end there.” It doesn’t.

entries.title: Children’s books roundup – the best new picture books and novels

Monster is FULL (of pizza!). An eye-wateringly bright board book, featuring splendidly zany, toddler-pleasing pairs of opposites.The Flying Machine of Dreams by Kate Wakeling, illustrated b
entries.content:
Small Monster, Big Monster by Allan Sanders, Phaidon, £7.95

Refrigerator is EMPTY. Monster is FULL (of pizza!). An eye-wateringly bright board book, featuring splendidly zany, toddler-pleasing pairs of opposites.

The Flying Machine of Dreams by Kate Wakeling, illustrated by Viviane Schwarz, Otter-Barry, £12.99

A delectable picture-book collaboration that perfectly distils the wonder of the everyday, from the textures of a leaf to a squishy-cushioned den. Wakeling’s irresistible poetry is richly heightened by Schwarz’s sweet, strange illustrations.

The Weather Shop by Thomas Lee, translated by Deborah Smith, Do Re Mi, £12.99

Translated from Korean, this intricate, inviting, Scarryesque picture book features a shop full of rain balloons, cloud pillows and snow sprays (and a sunshine scarf to warm everyone after the blizzard).

Bison Rule, OK! by Sarah Ziman, illustrated by Nia Havilliard, Otter-Barry, £8.99

What annoyed Big Sister this week? What’s the cure for everything in the school medical room? And what’s so good about having a bison as your friend? Witty, satisfying, resonant and fun, this enticing poetry collection will tempt a range of 6+ readers.

African Queens by Onyinye Iwu, Walker, £12.99

From Hatshepsut, the pharaoh her successors tried to erase, to Amanirenas, the Sudanese queen who fought the Romans and won, these strikingly illustrated stories of bold and fearless African rulers will grip 7+ history buffs.

The Palace of Facts by Kate Olesin, illustrated by Andy Smith, What on Earth Books, £22

This gigantic, spectacularly colourful nonfiction treasury is crammed with 400 facts, displayed in the Hall of Mirrors, the Fossil Hall, the Aquarium, the Maze (“The world’s largest maze, in Yancheng, China, is designed in the shape of an elk”) and many more. A rainy-day delight for trivia mavens of 7 or 8+.

Stableheart: Helping Hero by Nicci Johnson, S&S, £7.99

Sad to leave her foster parents and the pony she loved to ride, Pres isn’t yet ready to trust her Aunty Janelle, or form a new bond with the rescue pony at the city stables. But what if he really needs her? This heartwarming, layered, readable story will please 8+ horse lovers and Jacqueline Wilson fans.

How to Steal the Future by Christopher Edge, Macmillan, £7.99

At the heart of a dangerous, ever-changing maze hides the Avenir, a mystery with the power to unlock the future. Drew is looking for his sister Evie, who disappeared during her own attempt to reach the centre. As the traps and puzzles get deadlier, can Drew find Evie and save his own future before time runs out? A high-concept, brain-twisting 9+ thrill ride from the author of Escape Room.

Wilomina: The Land of Dreams and Nightmares by John Chalmers and Sandra Marrs, Scholastic, £9.99

On her way to visit Mum in hospital, a weird train ride strands Wilomina in a parallel world of dreams, where she befriends a talking cat, seeks out a mysterious library, and begins metamorphosing into a ferocious werepire. Fabulously odd, with a colour scheme of visceral purples and lurid greens, this surreal, gripping graphic novel will appeal to 9+ Ghibli fans.

My Name Is Zayn by Fidan Meikle, Floris, £7.99

After a long, dangerous journey fleeing the Taliban, Zayn is wrenched away from his best friend Samim when their dinghy sinks in the English Channel. Sent to a hotel housing other asylum seekers, Zayn’s attempts to start a new life are disrupted when his roommate disappears … A standalone companion to the award-winning My Name Is Samim, this moving, compelling 10+ story of courage and adaptability shines a searchlight on the asylum system and gangs who prey on vulnerable children.

Traitors’ Nest by Frances Hardinge, Macmillan, £16.99

In the kingdom of Thaletal, castles move as a Great Game is played, disrupting the lives of ordinary people. When teenage Burr’s village is threatened by an ominous new castle, a coup attempt backfires and Burr finds himself spirited away to an unknown corner of Thaletal. Can Burr and his sisters – and the strange heiress Burr has unwillingly kidnapped – learn to beat the players at their own Game? Humane, complex and inimitably inventive, this magnificent 12+ fantasy is yet another barnstormer from the Costa-winning Hardinge.

Cut Him Out in Little Stars by Lucy Strange, Chicken House, £8.99

When her fighter pilot fiance is shot down, heartbroken Juliet is sent to stay by the sea with her sister. But the discovery of a local girl’s body plunges her into mysteries past and present, and meeting handsome, scarred flight lieutenant Bertie Campbell complicates everything even more. Can Juliet overcome trauma and terror to risk falling in love again? This enchanting, atmospheric, poignant second world war romance is the brilliant Strange’s first foray into writing for teenagers.

Encore by Miles Toriko Burks, Farshore, £12.99

Kindergarten besties Clayton Noguchi and Aron Santos fell out in middle school; now they’ve unwillingly reunited in senior theatre class. As they navigate improv, drama games and conversations in and out of school, will they end up as friends – or something more? Based on a popular Webtoon, this funny, touching, addictive queer YA graphic novel should delight Heartstopper fans.

Hell to Pay by Lora Beth Johnson, Hot Key, £8.99

Accomplished thief Elle Fields steals secrets from the Dead, just like her brother used to, until a botched attempt cost him his soul. When charismatic stranger Rook offers her a commission promising a chance at resurrection, she can’t resist assembling her former crew for one last Afterlife heist. But there are things Elle doesn’t know about her brother’s death, or the job she’s accepted … Original and fast-paced, boasting taut characterisation and impressive emotional heft, this supernatural YA thriller will electrify Leigh Bardugo devotees.

entries.title: Kolkhoz by Emmanuel Carrère review – intricate portrait of an elite French family

entries.content:
When Emmanuel Carrère’s mother, Hélène, died in 2023, at the age of 94, President Macron spoke at her memorial. She had been “perpetual secretary” of the Académie Française, in effect its head, and 200 people gathered at Les Invalides in Paris to pay tribute. Emmanuel’s father, Louis, was there too, in a wheelchair, only half aware of what was going on. This 400-page memoir, translated into English by John Lambert, is a homage to both parents and the unlikely history that brought them together. It’s also an act of reparation towards Hélène, whom Emmanuel worshipped as a child but upset as an adult by publishing a book that she’d forbidden him to write.

Hélène grew up in stateless poverty in Paris, the daughter of Georges Zourabichvili, whose parents had fled Georgia in 1921, and Nathalie von Pelken, who as a child had six governesses, one for each day excluding Sunday. Though “the magical world of the fallen Russian aristocracy” was the backdrop, conditions were tough, not least after Georges disappeared in 1944, murdered by partisans for alleged Nazi collaboration. Hélène was 15 at the time and unsuccessfully tried to hide the truth about George’s death from her younger brother, Nicolas.

She was determined and highly ambitious. What she couldn’t excel at, she didn’t do. For a time she considered an acting career but found her metier as a Russian historian. It helped that she was charming and attractive, so much so that an Afghan pilot, on a flight from Tashkent to Paris via Tehran, first invited her to the cockpit, then landed the plane in Kabul in order to kidnap her. He kept her there for four days before a couple of US aid workers sneaked her away on a private plane.

By then she was married to Louis, who worked for an insurance company and was often away on business trips. At home Hélène ruled the roost and let Emmanuel and his two sisters sleep around her bed, a setup she called “kolkhoz”, the name for collective farms in the USSR. There was no television or radio; the children were made to read. Her son’s reading was strenuous: from Jules Verne and Alexander Dumas, he moved on to Dostoevsky at 13. His mother brought out his softer side – whenever she went away he’d write long letters saying how “horribly” he missed her.

He felt abandoned when she began receiving phone calls from a “Mr N” and had long furtive conversations with him. No less distraught, her husband threatened to kill himself. Hélène ended the affair to spare Louis but he “lost her love for ever” and moved from the marriage bed to a tiny room. Worse, she more or less stopped speaking to him, a habit that lasted to the end. When diagnosed with cancer and admitted to a palliative care home, she merely told him she’d be away at a conference.

The mother-son relationship remained close until Emmanuel published A Russian Novel, which explored the story of her father, Georges, which she had asked him not to tell (“It’s my story, not yours. Leave him where he is”). Publication was “a family cataclysm”; she blamed her brother Nicolas for helping with it. Though she did eventually forgive Emmanuel, her loyalty to Russia divided them. A week before the invasion of Ukraine she described Putin as “a rational man”, committed to good relations with Europe. Dismayed, Emmanuel visited Georgia, where his cousin Salome Zourabichvili had become president. A trip to Ukraine followed. He remains violently opposed to Putin.

What’s attractive about the book is its intimacy. If Hélène is a grand dame, her son enjoys the role of bon vivant, disclosing his drinking bouts, journalistic forays, failed relationships and blissful third marriage as well as his bipolar disorder. He’d like to write with “filial piety” and both his father’s genealogical research and his uncle Nicolas’s memoirs help him fill out the family story. But he also lets us in on his uncertainties as he proceeds: “what I’m hoping for is the unhoped for. We’ll see.”

His mother loved order and completeness. And at her memorial Macron praised her for finishing the latest Académie dictionary – a 40-year task – with the word zygomatique (an anatomical term). In reality, as she frustratedly told her son, they’d only reached zoo, with 62 more words to come, the last of them zz, onomatopoeia for sleep. She wouldn’t have slept well if she’d known this book was coming, but it’s an epic achievement and an honest, heartfelt account.
